title: How To Stand Like A Leader And Get Respect
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that physical bearing communicates leadership to students just as much as words do, and he breaks down five parts of the body that shape how a teacher is perceived. Feet planted shoulder-width apart signal commitment and certainty, while pacing or hiding one leg reads as fear. Level, centered hips convey patience, while a swayed hip reads as impatience or dislike of the class. Visible, naturally moving hands build trust and warmth, while pocketed or clasped hands read as evasive. Squared shoulders and a lifted chin project confidence, citing researcher Amy Cuddy's work on posture and performance, while stooped shoulders communicate defeat. Finally, holding brief eye contact rather than casting eyes down signals boldness and full commitment to one's authority. He closes by recommending teachers review this checklist every morning and hold a confident stance before students arrive to build the habit over time.
points: Feet planted shoulder-width apart signal commitment and confidence; pacing or hiding a leg reads as fear.
Centered, level hips convey patience, while a swayed hip communicates impatience and dislike toward students.
Visible, naturally moving hands build trust and warmth; hidden or pocketed hands read as evasive.
Squared shoulders and a lifted chin project confidence, citing Amy Cuddy's research that a two-minute 'superhero' stance improves performance.
Holding a beat of eye contact throughout the day signals boldness and full commitment to classroom authority.
quotes: How you present yourself to your students matters. The way you dress, speak, and move has an impact on how they view you and thus how they behave in your class.
This stance lets people know that you’re committed to your words and have confidence in yourself and what you’re saying. It reflects certainty over uncertainty.
Showing your hands makes you more trustworthy. Moving them to emphasize your points demonstrates warmth and enthusiasm.
Students don’t want to follow a weak-kneed underachiever or someone who stands like one. They have to believe in you.
Researcher Amy Cuddy discovered that if you stand like a superhero for just two minutes, you perform better.
Instead, make it a point to hold a beat of eye contact with all your students throughout each day. The more you do it, the easier it gets and more influence you’ll have.
